# Pre-lab Prep
## Multiple Regression: Simpson's Paradox

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(16))
```

## Choose our parameters

```{r}
B0 <- 10 # intercept
B1 <- 0.1 # Additional typo per increase in typing speed
B2 <- -10 # Difference between typist B and the reference level A
sigma <- 3 # Standard dev of the residuals
```

## Generate our predictors

Remember, for Simpson's paradox, there mus tbe a relationship between the predictors.

```{r}
# Sample size
N <- 30

# Typist identities
typist <- sample(c("A", "B"), N, replace = TRUE)

# Dummy variable for typist B
typistB <- ifelse(typist == "B", 1, 0)

# THIS IS THE KEY PART
# The continuous predictor variable is dependent on the categorical variable
typing_speed <- rnorm(N, mean = ifelse(typist == "B", 100, 45), sd = 15)
```

## Calculate expected value of the response
```{r}
expected_typos <- B0 + B1 * typing_speed + B2 * typistB
```

## Simulate the response variable

```{r}
typos <- rnorm(
    n = N,
    mean = expected_typos,
    sd = sigma
)
```

## Visualize!

```{r}
simulated_typing <- tibble(typing_speed, typos, typist)

ggplot(simulated_typing, aes(typing_speed, typos, fill = typist)) +
    geom_point(size = 2, shape = 21)
```

## Fit and interpret

If we only look at typing speed:


```{r}
one_predictor_lm <- lm(typos ~ typing_speed, simulated_typing)
summary(one_predictor_lm)
```
Output:

two_predictor_lm <- lm(typos ~ typing_speed + typist, simulated_typing)
summary(two_predictor_lm)
